bluf: Ukraine is stabilizing the frontline and making territorial gains, inflicting heavy casualties on Russian forces, while Russia conducts unannounced nuclear exercises with Belarus and fails to secure a key energy deal with China. Simultaneously, Iran is using ceasefire negotiations to normalize its control over the Strait of Hormuz, with NATO considering escort operations, and the US canceling a planned strike amid diplomatic efforts.

sections.title: Military Operations
sections.content: Ukraine continues to hold and stabilize the frontline, with Western officials and NATO reporting Ukrainian territorial gains following Russia's loss of Starlink access in February 2026. Ukrainian forces are conducting intensified long-range and mid-range strike campaigns, including a large-scale strike on May 16-17 against Russian defense industrial plants and oil infrastructure in Moscow City and Oblast, and a massive Russian strike on May 17-18 with 546 drones and missiles. Russian forces are suffering unsustainable losses—over 59,000 seriously wounded, 800 POWs, and an average of 1,021 casualties per day in 2026—while Russia uses unannounced strategic nuclear exercises with Belarus to posture strength and distract from battlefield weaknesses.
sources: Ukraine’s Fortress Belt: The Key to Sustaining the Frontline

sections.title: Political and Diplomatic Developments
sections.content: Russia's President Putin failed to secure a deal on the Power of Siberia-2 pipeline during his visit to China, signing only minor agreements, highlighting limits in Russo-Sino cooperation. The Kremlin remains committed to original war aims despite internal recognition of a 'dead end,' with Bloomberg reporting that Putin wants to seize Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts by end of 2026. Russia continues to deepen control over Belarus through joint nuclear exercises and constitutional changes, while occupation officials in Ukraine pursue forced transfers of children and integration into Russian systems. The US-Iran negotiations show 'slight progress' but remain stuck on Iran's HEU stockpile and Strait of Hormuz control, with Iran using the ceasefire to normalize its protection racket over the strait.

sections.title: Economic and Maritime Security
sections.content: Iran is institutionalizing its control over the Strait of Hormuz, charging vessels 'security' fees to avoid attacks, with Iranian officials coalescing around demands for formalized transit authority. The US is pressuring Iran through naval blockades and sanctions, seizing an Iranian-linked oil tanker, while South Korea considers joining the US-led Maritime Freedom Construct after an Iranian attack on a South Korean vessel. NATO countries reportedly support a plan to escort ships through the strait starting in July, but unanimous support is lacking. Russia's economic constraints are evident as it fails to secure the PS-2 pipeline deal with China, while Ukraine's mid-range strikes disrupt Russian logistics in occupied territories.

key_developments: Ukraine is making territorial gains and stabilizing the frontline, with Russian casualties averaging over 1,000 per day in 2026.
Russia conducted unannounced strategic nuclear exercises with Belarus, highlighting deepened de facto control over Belarus.
Putin failed to secure a Power of Siberia-2 pipeline deal with China, revealing limits in Russo-Sino cooperation.
Iran is using ceasefire negotiations to normalize control over the Strait of Hormuz, with NATO considering escort operations.
The US canceled a planned military strike on Iran on May 18 amid diplomatic efforts, but remains prepared for large-scale action.
outlook: Ukraine's defensive resilience and strike campaigns will likely continue to impose unsustainable costs on Russia, though the Kremlin remains committed to maximalist war aims. Iran's normalization of Strait of Hormuz control will face increasing international resistance, potentially escalating into a multinational naval confrontation if negotiations fail.
